Vaccine Vexation

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The plan was for 67% of the population to get Covid -19 vaccines by the end of this year. But while some nations have reached 40% coverage, we ask why are lagging at less than 1%

Unique Selling Point:
Vaccination Vexation

The South African Government has promised to have 67% of our population, or about 40 million South Africans vaccinated by the end of the year. This weekend President Cyril Ramaphosa, speaking at a Human Rights Day commemoration, again assured South Africans that every single person in the country would get access to a vaccine, and called for patience.

But there are growing concerns that the government's promised two thirds target by the end of the year won't happen. Especially since no one seems to be able to tell us how this will be achieved. In one of the worst public health disasters of the century, why all the secrecy? Or is it simply that they themselves don't know?

Summary:
To achieve the 67% target, we would need to ramp up daily vaccinations to about 250 000 doses, while at best we are currently only at about 10 000 a day. On Saturday Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize confirmed the total number of vaccines administered to date stood at 182 983 - most of these going to front-line health care workers. That is a far cry from the estimated 1.5 million doses needed to cover all our health care providers, a target that was set for the end of April this year.

So what is the hold up and how can it be fixed?
That's a question only government can answer at this stage. There is a confirmed world wide shortage of vaccines, and many first world countries have been accused of ordering too many vaccines ( countries like the US have ordered 1 billion for their 330 million population) and hoarding vaccines not needed. There are also issues over the question of vaccine efficacy and safety, as well as which ones to procure for SA. We have only recently concluded the sale of the Astra-Zeneca vaccines we bought to AU member countries, after it was decided to halt the use of the vaccine because of questions around its usefulness against the South African strain of Covid-19 (A decision that has been questioned by many experts).

Meanwhile, government has said they will NOT force anyone to take the vaccine - but there is a growing worldwide trend to require people to have "vaccine passports", proving they've been vaccinated before they are allowed to enter work premises, hotels etc. So while the government might not force us, could private institutions soon require it? And will South Africans who have not been vaccinated be allowed to work and travel to countries where such restrictions are in place?



Further information:
With a 3rd wave of Covid infections predicted for early June, in a country which saw 22 000 infections a day at it's zenith, can we afford for government not to have a clearly defined vaccine roll out strategy in place?

Insert Elements
- Get an answer from government or the Dept of Health. The minister has spoken to us before and hopefully will again.
- Speak to Prof Salim Abdool Karim, co-chairperson of the Ministerial Advisory Committee on what info they have re vaccine roll out.
- Try to get Prof Glenda Gray to speak to us - re Sisonky study of the Johnson Johnson vaccine.
- Interview Mario Christodoulou from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness and Innovation (CEPI) who are advocating against the hoarding of vaccines by first world countries - especially since to end the pandemic we need to end the disease worldwide.
-Interview Dr Stavros Nicolau, Senior Executive from Aspen Pharmacare, who have a deal to manufacture the vaccine in Port Elizabeth, get onto the plant?
- Look into the new Biovac deal - a Cape Town based pharmaceutical company who will be manufacturing Immunity Bio's second generation vaccine (which will reportedly be more effective against multiple strains, especially the SA one).
- Make the point that it's not just the third wave we face, Covid 19 has caused more than 50 000 deaths in Sa in only 12 months. That's equal to about 4200 deaths a month, or 136 people every day. If we were to report on an airplane falling from the sky with 136 people on board every day, we would be fixing the problem immediately. Why are we not doing so with our vaccines?

Mr. Steven Saad CEO Aspen
Prof. Shabir Mahdi Vaccines and Infectious Diseases Wits
Dr. Zweli Mkhize Minister of Health

Press Release:


Things We Lost in the Fire

As Cape Town firefighters continue trying to control the fires around Table Mountain, the international academic community has responded with shock and sadness to the monumental damage to property and legacy that the University of Cape Town has suffered. Carte Blanche sifts through the ashes as experts in charge of the unique and priceless archives of personal papers and plant specimens dating back to the 1800s evaluate the impact of the fires. From rescuing irreplaceable struggle history documents to religious texts – we recount some of the week’s courageous acts.

Producer: Liz Fish | Researcher: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


Vaccine Vexation
21 April 2021
First Draft Script

Voice
In the last few weeks we have had some good news around government’s Covid-19 vaccine rollout. The country has secured enough doses to vaccinate most of the population, millions of vaccines will be manufactured right here in South Africa, and the government’s online registration system is now open to senior citizens above the age of 60.

Link Bongani
But despite all the good news, the story of this vaccine roll out has been one of false starts. We’ve set ambitious targets, 40 million by the end of the year, a million health workers before the end of March, but we’ve been unable to fulfil them.

Voice
The stark reality is that so far, not a single ordinary South African has received a vaccine. We’ve only been able to give about 300 000 jabs to our more than one million healthcare workers - people over 60 will only start getting theirs from the 17th of May!

One man who’s been vocal in his criticism of the slow pace of the roll out has been Professor of Vaccinology at Wits University, Shabir Madhi.

Sound Up Madhi
Madhi: So any plan to start rolling out vaccine is very welcome, but at the same time I think the roll out of the vaccine is going to be somewhat late.

Voice
The former member of the Ministerial Advisory Committee on Covid-19 says the 17th of May, the official start date for those over 60, is around the same time many experts are predicting the dreaded third wave, a resurgence in Corona Virus infections.

Sound Up Madhi
For these vaccines to work, you need to have at least a 14 day period, before the vaccine really starts kicking in, vaccinating in the midst of a resurgence is simply not going to have much benefit during the course of that particular wave.

Voice
Currently less than one percent of our population has been immunised, whilst a country like Israel announced this week people there no longer have to wear masks outdoors, having vaccinated more than half of all adults. Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize says things should start moving a lot faster come mid May.

Sound Up Dr Zweli Mkhize
Bongani: Minister, once people have been registered, there’s been a sense of apprehension around not knowing some of the details, in other words if I were to register for example, what number would I be in the queue, what sight would have been identified for me to go and get vaccinated, how will all of that work?

Zweli: The Electronic Vaccination Data System is trying to establish the location of the individuals, so it should be able to indicate the nearest facility nearby, and therefore send a message to say your center is in such and such an area, based on your address that you’d have given.

Voice
The Electronic Vaccination Data System seems to be running smoothly – with the roughly 350 000 people who have registered so far being told they’ll be notified of the next steps via sms.

Government has been criticised for the lack of granular detail to the roll out plan, but here’s what we know so far. We’ve secured 31.2 million units of the single dose Johnson & Johnson vaccine, and another 30 million double dose vaccines from Pfizer.

Sound Up Zweli Mkhize
Which means together the two, will be able to give us 46 million vaccines.

Voice
Phase two of the roll out will target 16.5 million people, and will last from mid May to mid October.
That will include the roughly five and a half million people over 60 years of age and hopefully all our healthcare workers. The remainder of the phase two vaccines will go to people over the age of 40 who are frontline workers or have co-morbidities, and government will announce when they can register.

Sound Up Zweli Mkhize
The next highest level of ill health, severity of disease, hospitalisation is among those who are 40 years and above.

Voice
Over 2000 sites have been designated for vaccine distribution. The EVDS will notify you when it’s your time to go, vaccines are not mandatory, no one will have to pay to receive one, and the minister is urging every South African to get their vaccine.

Sound Up Zweli Mkhize
We encourage people, for their own safety, and for the sake of their own health, that they must use the vaccines.

Link Bongani
So how safe are these vaccines, that’s the million dollar question. Because without it, life is not going to return to normal. And places like this that used to be pumping, and full of people, are going to stay empty.

Voice
On the 13th of April the Minister announced that South Africa would temporarily suspend it’s Johnson & Johnson vaccine roll out, off the back of concerns emanating from America.

Professor Helen Rees is the Chairperson of the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority, or SAHPRA.

Sound Up Prof Helen Rees
Bongani: Professor Rees, the pause on the J&J vaccine rollout has now been lifted, there are those who are critical of that decision in the first instance, saying it was just extreme caution.

Helen: It certainly was cautionary. We received reports from the United States of a very rare condition, that combined thrombosis in the brain, with something called low platelets, which is part of your clotting mechanism, this is a very rare condition and there were six cases, but out of nearly 7 million people who’d been immunised.


Voice
There is currently no proof the blood clotting events were caused by the vaccine. But even if they were, you are far more likely to develop blood clots from a Covid-19 infection than from getting vaccinated.

Sound Up Prof Helen Rees
The benefit from stopping yourself from getting Covid infection, greatly outweighs the risk of the vaccine.

Link Bongani
It’s safe to say very little about this virus has been predictable. The countries that were expected to do well, have been some of the countries that have struggled the most. So yes South Africa has met it’s fair share of challenges, but we are not the only ones. And now the challenge is some of those countries that do have the resources, want to keep them for themselves.

Sound Up Helen Rees
We saw this in Europe, not wanting to export the AstraZeneca to the UK, but now we’ve seen there’s a huge wave of infection in India. Now we’re seeing the Indian government saying, listen, we now have to prioritise the Indian population, because we’re under huge pressure, so that could also become a barrier if countries that manufacture, are under domestic pressure themselves, and exports stop. Sow we’re going to have to watch all of these things.

Link Bongani
Securing the vaccine is one thing, now the world faces the biggest logistical challenge we have ever encountered, because the vaccines are going to be useless if they don’t get into the arms of the people who need them.

Voice
The partnership between the private and public sectors will play a crucial part in any successful roll out. One of the major local players will be pharmaceutical giant Aspen Pharmacare. Stephen Saad is the CEO.

Sound Up Stephen
Bongani: So what is the Aspen facility offering South Africa?

Stephen: I think the Aspen facility offers South Africa absolute vaccine security of supply.

Voice
President Ramaphosa and Minister Mkhize visited Aspen’s manufacturing facility in Gqeberha just before Easter. There it was announced that at least half of the South African population would be receiving Johnson and Johnson vaccines manufactured at the plant. Saad is confident that they’ll be able to meet the national demand.

Sound Up Stephen
Aspen can make nearly a million doses a day, probably our capacity is at 25 million doses a month. I mean that’s very big capacity, it’s more than we could ever roll out.

Voice
One of the concerns around the Pfizer vaccine is that it must be stored at ultra low temperatures, but Beyond Wireless CEO Ian Lester says that’s only during bulk storage.

Sound Up Ian Lester
As far as bulk storage is concerned, vaccines like Pfizer, and there are others, need to be stored at ultra low temperatures, so minus 70 degrees.


Voice
Lester is the man behind this homegrown device known as the ICE3, which can remotely monitor vaccine temperature’s anywhere across the globe - and has a battery life of 5 years from a single charge.

Sound Up Ian Lester
However, when they come out of those depots they are perfectly stable for prolonged periods of time in the case of Pfizer for up to 5 days at 2 to 8 degrees celsius.

Voice
The ICE3 allows distributors to see the exact temperature of a batch of vaccines at any given time, and can even sound the alarm if a consignment deviates from a given route, as it also uses gps to track location. And they’re already in use right here in South Africa.

Sound Up Ian Lester
Companies like Dischem, Dischem Distribution, United Pharmaceutical Distributors which is part of the Click’s group, so encouragingly there are already several companies in South Africa that are already using this technology and have been using it for some time.

Voice
Professor Madhi says like it or not, Covid-19 is not going anywhere anytime soon.

Sound Up Prof Madhi
The virus is going to continue circulating. And that is something we need to start developing some comfort with. That this virus is not going to go away, it’s going to be here for the rest of our lifetimes.

Voice
And while the current batch of vaccines might not protect you from contracting Covid-19, they will protect you from severe disease, hospitlisation, and death.

Sound Up Prof Madhi
For me a good case scenario is getting to where we are with seasonal influenza, which each year kills roughly about ten to eleven thousand South Africans. And the way to get to that good case scenario is to ensure that we can get the high risk population vaccinated as quickly as possible. To protect them, not against infection, but to protect them from being hospitalised and dying from the illness.



Promo 1
Israel has vaccinated more than half of all their adults, South Africa is lagging at less than one percent. We take a closer look at our long awaited vaccine roll out.

Promo 2
As online registrations for senior citizens to receive their Covid-19 vaccinations go live, is South Africa is doing enough to protect the most vulnerable from the dreaded 3rd wave?

Promo 3
We ask experts if there are any causes for concern around South Africa’s Covid-19 vaccines, and find out how soon you will be eligible to receive your life saving shot.

Link Bongani Securing the vaccine is one thing, now the world faces the biggest logistical challenge we have ever encountered, because the vaccines are going to be useless if they don’t get into the arms of the people who need them. Voice The partnership between the private and public sectors will play a crucial part in any successful roll out. One of the major local players will be pharmaceutical giant Aspen Pharmacare. Stephen Saad is the CEO. Sound Up Stephen Bongani: So what is the Aspen facility offering South Africa? Stephen: I think the Aspen facility offers South Africa absolute vaccine security of supply. Voice President Ramaphosa and Minister Mkhize visited Aspen’s manufacturing facility in Gqeberha just before Easter. There it was announced that at least half of the South African population would be receiving Johnson and Johnson vaccines manufactured at the plant. Saad is confident that they’ll be able to meet the national demand. Sound Up Stephen Aspen can make nearly a million doses a day, probably our capacity is at 25 million doses a month. I mean that’s very big capacity, it’s more than we could ever roll out. Voice One of the concerns around the Pfizer vaccine is that it must be stored at ultra low temperatures, but Beyond Wireless CEO Ian Lester says that’s only during bulk storage. Sound Up Ian Lester As far as bulk storage is concerned, vaccines like Pfizer, and there are others, need to be stored at ultra low temperatures, so minus 70 degrees. Voice Lester is the man behind this homegrown device known as the ICE3, which can remotely monitor vaccine temperature’s anywhere across the globe - and has a battery life of 5 years from a single charge. Sound Up Ian Lester However, when they come out of those depots they are perfectly stable for prolonged periods of time in the case of Pfizer for up to 5 days at 2 to 8 degrees celsius. Voice The ICE3 allows distributors to see the exact temperature of a batch of vaccines at any given time, and can even sound the alarm if a consignment deviates from a given route, as it also uses gps to track location. And they’re already in use right here in South Africa. Sound Up Ian Lester Companies like Dischem, Dischem Distribution, United Pharmaceutical Distributors which is part of the Click’s group, so encouragingly there are already several companies in South Africa that are already using this technology and have been using it for some time. Voice Professor Madhi says like it or not, Covid-19 is not going anywhere anytime soon. Sound Up Prof Madhi The virus is going to continue circulating. And that is something we need to start developing some comfort with. That this virus is not going to go away, it’s going to be here for the rest of our lifetimes. Voice And while the current batch of vaccines might not protect you from contracting Covid-19, they will protect you from severe disease, hospitlisation, and death. Sound Up Prof Madhi For me a good case scenario is getting to where we are with seasonal influenza, which each year kills roughly about ten to eleven thousand South Africans. And the way to get to that good case scenario is to ensure that we can get the high risk population vaccinated as quickly as possible. To protect them, not against infection, but to protect them from being hospitalised and dying from the illness. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The plan was for 67% of the population to get Covid -19 vaccines by the end of this year. But while some nations have reached 40% coverage, we ask why are lagging at less than 1%
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Vaccination Vexation The South African Government has promised to have 67% of our population, or about 40 million South Africans vaccinated by the end of the year. This weekend President Cyril Ramaphosa, speaking at a Human Rights Day commemoration, again assured South Africans that every single person in the country would get access to a vaccine, and called for patience. But there are growing concerns that the government's promised two thirds target by the end of the year won't happen. Especially since no one seems to be able to tell us how this will be achieved. In one of the worst public health disasters of the century, why all the secrecy? Or is it simply that they themselves don't know?
metadata.Summary: To achieve the 67% target, we would need to ramp up daily vaccinations to about 250 000 doses, while at best we are currently only at about 10 000 a day. On Saturday Minister of Health Dr Zweli Mkhize confirmed the total number of vaccines administered to date stood at 182 983 - most of these going to front-line health care workers. That is a far cry from the estimated 1.5 million doses needed to cover all our health care providers, a target that was set for the end of April this year. So what is the hold up and how can it be fixed? That's a question only government can answer at this stage. There is a confirmed world wide shortage of vaccines, and many first world countries have been accused of ordering too many vaccines ( countries like the US have ordered 1 billion for their 330 million population) and hoarding vaccines not needed. There are also issues over the question of vaccine efficacy and safety, as well as which ones to procure for SA. We have only recently concluded the sale of the Astra-Zeneca vaccines we bought to AU member countries, after it was decided to halt the use of the vaccine because of questions around its usefulness against the South African strain of Covid-19 (A decision that has been questioned by many experts). Meanwhile, government has said they will NOT force anyone to take the vaccine - but there is a growing worldwide trend to require people to have "vaccine passports", proving they've been vaccinated before they are allowed to enter work premises, hotels etc. So while the government might not force us, could private institutions soon require it? And will South Africans who have not been vaccinated be allowed to work and travel to countries where such restrictions are in place?
metadata.Further information: With a 3rd wave of Covid infections predicted for early June, in a country which saw 22 000 infections a day at it's zenith, can we afford for government not to have a clearly defined vaccine roll out strategy in place? Insert Elements - Get an answer from government or the Dept of Health. The minister has spoken to us before and hopefully will again. - Speak to Prof Salim Abdool Karim, co-chairperson of the Ministerial Advisory Committee on what info they have re vaccine roll out. - Try to get Prof Glenda Gray to speak to us - re Sisonky study of the Johnson Johnson vaccine. - Interview Mario Christodoulou from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness and Innovation (CEPI) who are advocating against the hoarding of vaccines by first world countries - especially since to end the pandemic we need to end the disease worldwide. -Interview Dr Stavros Nicolau, Senior Executive from Aspen Pharmacare, who have a deal to manufacture the vaccine in Port Elizabeth, get onto the plant? - Look into the new Biovac deal - a Cape Town based pharmaceutical company who will be manufacturing Immunity Bio's second generation vaccine (which will reportedly be more effective against multiple strains, especially the SA one). - Make the point that it's not just the third wave we face, Covid 19 has caused more than 50 000 deaths in Sa in only 12 months. That's equal to about 4200 deaths a month, or 136 people every day. If we were to report on an airplane falling from the sky with 136 people on board every day, we would be fixing the problem immediately. Why are we not doing so with our vaccines?
